You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: low frequency, mid load; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 680 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: high frequency, small Cp, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 17.5 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: low frequency, large Cp; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: high frequency, large Cp, heavy load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: hot, heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 200 kOhm, temperature 85 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:

S2       2.04    2.09    83.1   0.518      6.14  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S3        4.2    4.21    23.2  0.0865      3.75  ok       FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL

S5       1.74    1.74    8.96       -      20.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6       1.55    1.56    25.4       -        12  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",

      "pzp",

     ],

    },
    {

      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",

     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],

    },
    {
     "id": "S1",

     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 3 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo energy harvester.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (settled mean).
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (absolute max).
        *   Ripple $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (0.7-0.8s).
        *   Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$.
        *   Settled $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (stability between 0.6-0.7s and 0.7-0.8s).
    *   Piezo Model: Sinusoidal current $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$ (S1).

    *   S1: Nominal.
    *   S2: Low freq (50Hz), mid load ($680\text{ k}\Omega$).
    *   S3: High freq (200Hz), small $C_p$ (17.5nF), light load ($4.7\text{ M}\Omega$).
    *   S4: Low freq (50Hz), large $C_p$ (32.5nF), load $1\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   S5: High freq (200Hz), large $C_p$ (32.5nF), heavy load ($150\text{ k}\Omega$).
    *   S6: Hot (85C), heavy load ($200\text{ k}\Omega$).

    *   `fbr_zener` (Full-bridge rectifier + Zener clamp):
        *   S1, S2, S3, S4: OK.
        *   S5: $V_{avg} = 1.73\text{ V}$ (FAIL), Startup (FAIL).
        *   S6: $V_{avg} = 1.55\text{ V}$ (FAIL), Startup (FAIL).
        *   Reason: Inefficient power transfer for heavy loads (S5, S6). The FBR is passive and doesn't optimize the extraction from $C_p$.
    *   `p_sshi_zener` (Parallel SSHI - Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor):
        *   The provided topology was an FBR with an inductor-switch loop.
        *   S5: $V_{avg} = 3.3\text{ V}$ (OK), but ripple and stability (FAIL).
        *   S2, S4, S6: $V_{avg} < 1.8\text{ V}$ (FAIL).
        *   Reason: Poor configuration or tuning. The SSHI usually boosts efficiency significantly by inverting the voltage on $C_p$.
    *   `full_wave_doubler`: Failed screening.

    *   The FBR fails on heavy loads (S5, S6) because the voltage drop across diodes and the lack of $C_p$ energy recovery limit the output voltage.
    *   To improve power extraction from a piezo, SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) is the standard.
    *   Standard SSHI: At the peak of the piezo voltage, an inductor is switched in parallel with $C_p$ to flip the voltage, effectively increasing the charge transferred to the rectifier.
    *   Let's try a **proper SSHI circuit**.
    *   Circuit components for SSHI:
        *   Rectifier: FBR (4 diodes).
        *   Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
        *   The switch should close at the voltage peaks.
        *   The switch should be closed for a time $t_{on} \approx \frac{\pi}{2} \sqrt{LC_p}$ (though the prompt says $\pi\sqrt{LC_p}$, usually it's $\pi/2$ for a half-cycle flip, but I'll use the hint provided).

    *   Piezo nodes: `pzp`, `pzn`.
    *   Rectifier:
        *   D1: `pzp` -> `out`
        *   D2: `pzn` -> `out`
        *   D3: `0` -> `pzp`
        *   D4: `0` -> `pzn`
    *   SSHI Flip:
        *   Inductor L1: `pzp` -> `n1`
        *   Switch S1: `n1` -> `pzn`
        *   Controller G1: `edges: both` (flips at both positive and negative peaks).
    *   Storage:
        *   Capacitor Cout: `out` -> `0`.
    *   Protection:
        *   Zener DZ1: `0` -> `out` (cathode on `out`).

    *Wait*, if the rectifier is already there, the SSHI switch $S_1$ connects $L_1$ across the piezo.
    When $S_1$ closes, $C_p$ discharges through $L_1$ and $S_1$, creating an LC oscillation that flips the voltage on $C_p$.

    *Let's check the `p_sshi_zener` attempt again.*
    `D1 D pzp out DSCH`, `D2 D pzn out DSCH`, `D3 D 0 pzp DSCH`, `D4 D 0 pzn DSCH` (Full Bridge)
    `L1 L pzp n1 0.01`, `S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1`
    Wait, this is exactly what I just described. Why did it fail?
    `cond S1 vavg 1.97 vmax 2.09 vpp 237 tup 0.678`
    `S2 vavg 0.99 vmax 1.06 vpp 134`
    `S4 vavg 0.984 vmax 1.05 vpp 134`
    `S6 vavg 1.39 vmax 1.46 vpp 150`
    The ripple was huge (237 mV) and $V_{avg}$ was too low for low-frequency cases (S2, S4).
    Looking at `p_sshi_zener`'s `C1` value: `1e-05`.
    For S2, $R_L = 680\text{ k}\Omega$. With a pulse every $1/100\text{s}$ (S1) or $1/50\text{s}$ (S2), $C_{out}$ might need to be larger to reduce ripple, but $10\text{ uF}$ should be plenty.
    Wait, the `p_sshi_zener` results show `S5 vavg 3.3 V`. S5 is high frequency and heavy load. The SSHI is definitely working there.
    The failure in S2, S4, S6 for `p_sshi_zener` is likely due to the inductor value ($10\text{ mH}$) and $t_{on}$ not being optimized for the different $C_p$ and frequencies, or perhaps the bridge diodes are too restrictive.

    Wait, the `fbr_zener` (no SSHI) was actually better for S2 and S4!
    `fbr_zener`: S2 $V_{avg} = 2.29\text{ V}$, S4 $V_{avg} = 1.94\text{ V}$.
    `p_sshi_zener`: S2 $V_{avg} = 0.99\text{ V}$, S4 $V_{avg} = 0.98\text{ V}$.
    This is strange. SSHI should always be more efficient than FBR.
    Wait! If the inductor is too large or $t_{on}$ is too long, it might be shorting the piezo for too long or causing huge losses.
    Or, if the inductor is too large, the resonance frequency $1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC_p})$ is too low, and the voltage flip doesn't happen correctly within the $t_{on}$ window.

    Let's look at the `p_sshi_zener` again.
    `L1 = 10 mH`, `ton = 49.7 us`.
    $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$.
    $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC_p} = 1/\sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = 1/\sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-10}} = 1 / (1.58 \cdot 10^{-5}) \approx 63245\text{ rad/s}$.
    $T_0 = 2\pi / \omega_0 \approx 99\text{ us}$.
    A half-period is $\approx 50\text{ us}$.
    $t_{on} = 49.7\text{ us}$ is almost exactly a half-period.
    This should flip the voltage.

    Why did `fbr_zener` outperform `p_sshi_zener` on S2/S4?
    S2: $f = 50\text{ Hz}$, $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$.
    S4: $f = 50\text{ Hz}$, $C_p = 32.5\text{ nF}$.
    Maybe the inductor's series resistance is the killer?
    $L = 10\text{ mH} \implies R_{series} = 2 + 5 \cdot 10 = 52\text{ }\Omega$.
    In SSHI, the energy stored in $C_p$ is moved to the inductor and then to the rectifier.
    The energy lost in $R_{series}$ is $E_{loss} = \int i^2 R dt$.
    Peak current $I_{peak} \approx V_{oc} \sqrt{C_p/L}$.
    For S2: $I_{peak} \approx 3.2 \cdot \sqrt{25\text{n}/10\text{m}} = 3.2 \cdot \sqrt{2.5\cdot 10^{-6}} = 3.2 \cdot 1.58\text{ mA} \approx 5\text{ mA}$.
    This doesn't seem like enough to destroy the performance.

    Let's try a different approach. Maybe the SSHI isn't needed for all cases, but we need a more efficient rectifier or a better way to handle the heavy loads (S5, S6).
    Wait, the `fbr_zener` was only failing S5 and S6 slightly.
    S5: $V_{avg} = 1.73\text{ V}$ (need 1.8 V).
    S6: $V_{avg} = 1.55\text{ V}$ (need 1.8 V).
    S6 is "hot", meaning the diode drops might be lower, but the load is heavy ($200\text{ k}\Omega$).
    The problem is simply that the FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) has two diode drops in the path.
    $V_{out} \approx V_{peak} - 2V_f$.
    If $V_{peak}$ of the piezo is $3.2\text{ V}$ and $2V_f \approx 0.5\text{ V}$, $V_{out} \approx 2.7\text{ V}$.
    But this is the *peak*. The *average* voltage depends on the load.
    For heavy loads, the $C_{out}$ discharges more between cycles.

    Could we use a **Half-Bridge Rectifier** or a **Charge Pump**?
    A half-bridge would have only one diode drop but only uses half the cycles.
    What about a **Synchronous Rectifier**? We have `S` switches.
    If we use switches instead of diodes, we can eliminate the $V_f$ drop.

    Wait, the `S` switches are controlled by `SYNC`, which triggers at the extrema.
    We could build a synchronous rectifier.
    Positive half-cycle: $S_1$ closes, connecting `pzp` to `out`.
    Negative half-cycle: $S_2$ closes, connecting `pzn` to `out`.
    But we also need to connect the other side to ground.
    $S_3$ closes `pzn` to `0` during positive half-cycle.
    $S_4$ closes `pzp` to `0` during negative half-cycle.

    Let's try a **Synchronous Full Bridge Rectifier**.
    - S1: `pzp` to `out`, `ctrl=G1`, `edges=pos`
    - S2: `pzn` to `out`, `ctrl=G2`, `edges=neg`
    - S3: `pzn` to `0`, `ctrl=G1`, `edges=pos`
    - S4: `pzp` to `0`, `ctrl=G2`, `edges=neg`
    - G1: `edges=pos`, `ton=...`
    - G2: `edges=neg`, `ton=...`
    - $C_{out}$: `out` to `0`.
    - DZ1: `0` to `out` (clamp).

    Wait, the `S` switches have $R_{on} = 2\text{ }\Omega$. That's much better than a diode drop.
    And `ton` can be up to $1\text{ ms}$. For $100\text{ Hz}$, the half-period is $5\text{ ms}$. $1\text{ ms}$ is enough to transfer the charge.

    Wait, let's refine the Synchronous Rectifier.
    `SYNC` closes switches for `ton` seconds at the extrema.
    At the positive peak (extrema), the voltage is max. We want to transfer charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.
    So at the positive peak:
    - Switch `pzp` to `out`
    - Switch `pzn` to `0`
    At the negative peak:
    - Switch `pzn` to `out`
    - Switch `pzp` to `0`

    This is a synchronous bridge. Let's see if it's viable.
    Wait, the `SYNC` controller triggers at the *extrema*. The extrema are the *peaks* of the voltage.
    If we only close the switch for $1\text{ ms}$ at the peak, we only get a small pulse of current.
    The diodes in the FBR work for the *entire half-cycle*.
    The `S` switches are not meant to replace the diodes in a rectifier because they only stay closed for `ton` (max $1\text{ ms}$), while the half-cycle is $2.5\text{--}10\text{ ms}$.
    So a synchronous rectifier using `S` switches as described would be very inefficient.

    What about a **Synchronous SSHI**?
    The `p_sshi_zener` used an FBR for rectification and a switch for the flip.
    Maybe the issue was the $L$ value or $t_{on}$.
    Let's try a **different SSHI topology** or a **simpler one**.
    Maybe a **Voltage Doubler**? The user tried a full-wave doubler and it failed screening.

    Let's look at the FBR results again.
    S5: $V_{avg} = 1.73\text{ V}$ (FAIL)
    S6: $V_{avg} = 1.55\text{ V}$ (FAIL)
    S6 is the hardest. $R_L = 200\text{ k}\Omega$, $I_p = 50\text{ uA}$, $f = 100\text{ Hz}$, $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$.
